sentences: Out of the darkness, three figures are locked together in a single, desperate knot.
Artemisia Gentileschi painted this around 1620, and it is counted among the most resolute scenes in all of Baroque painting.
In this story from the Apocrypha, the widow Judith slips into the tent of Holofernes, the general sent to besiege her city, and cuts off his head.
He had drunk heavily and fallen asleep; now he struggles desperately.
Above, her young maid pins down the struggling man with her whole body, while his fist pushes up beneath her chin.
Earlier painters usually showed the maid as an old woman; here she is young, strong and fully involved.
On the right, Judith has rolled up her sleeves like someone setting to work.
Her strong arms and set face show no hesitation.
One hand grips his hair, and the other holds the sword firmly as she cuts.
Out of the darkness, all the arms converge on the centre and lead the eye straight to the blade.
The sword stands almost upright, and some read the shape of its hilt as an allusion to the cross.
A gold bracelet glints on Judith's wrist.
Blood has spattered up as far as her breast, yet her arm holds his head down without the slightest tremor.
Her rich golden dress and the brutal act make an unsettling pair.
Artemisia had painted the subject before, and in this second version the blood spurts from the neck in clean arcs.
Some historians link those arcs to the studies of motion by Galileo, her friend and correspondent.
Holofernes's head is thrown back, his eyes wide with terror, his upside-down face turned toward us.
Dark blood runs down and spreads across the white sheets, a stark and shocking contrast of red and white.
At the left, the red cloth and white sheets leap out of the dark, and his raised knee shows how hard he is kicking.
This dramatic play of light and shadow carries the strong influence of Caravaggio, whose work she knew well.
The price for this commission was agreed with Grand Duke Cosimo II de' Medici in Florence, who died soon after the canvas was finished.
She was paid only after a long and difficult delay, with help from her friend Galileo.
Its raw force once kept it off the gallery walls, but today the canvas hangs in the Uffizi alongside works by Caravaggio.
Step back and look again at how calm and steady the two women's arms are.
